lesson.menu_title: It Was the Contract That Changed Everything

lesson.subtitle: Lesson 7 -- It Was the Contract That Changed Everything
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Ladeia Tavares | Lesson 7 -- It Was the Contract That Changed Everything

listenings.text: Put six issues on a table and watch what happens. Five of them are noise. The room will spend its afternoon on whichever one was mentioned first, which is almost never the one that decides anything, and everybody will go home believing they worked hard. So I teach one question, and I teach it before anything else, because it does most of the work on its own. If everything else went your way, would you sign today? That is it. Ask it slowly and then be quiet. What that question does is make the other side name the crux themselves, and nobody feels they have given anything away by answering it, because on the surface you have offered them everything. Half the time the answer surprises them as much as it surprises you. And here is the part my students never believe until it happens to them. The people who are good at this are not quicker, and they are not cleverer. They simply say the sentence out loud. Most people never do, because naming the real issue feels like showing your hand, and it is the opposite: it is the only move that gives you the rest of the session to solve it.

People hear the word reframing and they think manipulation, so let me give you the plainest example I have. A musician wanted out of a contract. Her lawyer called it a release. The other side could not agree to a release, not because of her, but because eleven other artists were on the same clause and a release would have bound them. So somebody in the room called it a renegotiation instead. Not one fact changed. What changed was what the other side was able to say yes to. Now, is that dishonest? I would say the opposite, and here is why. Every description is a choice. The first description in the room was also a choice, and nobody examined it, and it happened to be the one that made agreement impossible. Pretending that there is a neutral way to describe a dispute is the only genuinely dishonest position available. And there is one more thing this gives you, especially if you are young and the room is not listening to you. The long form announces that something important is coming. What she wants is. The reason we are here is. That half second is enough for a room to stop talking, and you cannot buy it any other way.

Ask anybody where a negotiation is most likely to collapse and they will tell you the beginning, over the big difference, the gap that looks impossible on the first morning. The evidence says otherwise. Most of them die in the last five per cent, when the two sides are close enough to see the end, and that pattern holds across commercial disputes, employment cases and international agreements alike. The explanation is not mysterious. The issue that nobody named at the beginning is still sitting there at the end, and by that point both sides have spent everything they had to trade on the five things that were easier to talk about. There is nothing left to solve the hard one with, and there is no time either. We asked a researcher who has studied failed negotiations for two decades what she would change. Her answer took four seconds. Name the hardest issue in the first twenty minutes. What gets in the way, she said, is that it feels like weakness, and it is the exact opposite: it is the only decision that gives you the whole session to work on the thing that is actually going to decide it.
